clue.text: Inspiration from the bar, drunk!

indicators.note: someone drunk is all over the place, so the letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, six letters

explanation.surface: A tipsy drinker claims to find their creative inspiration propping up the pub bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspiration here is the physical act of drawing air into the lungs, not a creative spark.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspiration in its medical sense is inhaling, and an intake of air into the lungs is exactly that.

clue.text: Beg for starter of bacon and cheese crackers

indicators.note: a starter is what comes first, so only the opening letter is kept
crackers means crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone pleads for a snack of bacon-and-cheese crackers to start the meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Crackers looks like the biscuits being begged for, but it is the signal to scramble the cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: To beseech someone is to implore or entreat them urgently, which is pleading with them.

clue.text: Happening to be seventy without clothing

indicators.note: undressed means stripped of its outer layer, so the outside letters are removed

blocks.note: the word with its first and last letters stripped away

explanation.surface: A cheeky septuagenarian decides to celebrate turning seventy by going naked.
explanation.walkthrough: Stripping a word means losing its outer letters, here the S and Y around the inside of seventy.
explanation.definitionFit: A happening is an occurrence or incident, a thing that takes place, which is what an event is.

clue.text: Different alert sign shapes

indicators.note: making something different changes it, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, nine letters

explanation.surface: Warning signs come in various different shapes.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, British road warning signs are themselves triangular.
explanation.definitionFit: Triangles are three-sided figures, one kind of geometric shape, so the plural fits by example.

clue.text: Is youngster able to eat here?

definitions.note: a verb phrase pointing to a place where people eat

blocks.note: being able to do something means you can
a teenager, shortened

explanation.surface: A worried parent asks whether a child is allowed to eat at this place.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the question as 'Can teen eat here?': the two words of wordplay swap order because of the question form.
explanation.definitionFit: A canteen is a dining room in a school, factory or office where meals are served, a place to eat.

clue.text: Actors call for throwing out lines

definitions.note: a noun phrase for the process of choosing actors

blocks.note: first meaning: the selection of performers for roles
second meaning: what an angler does with a fishing line

explanation.walkthrough: Lines suggests an actor's script, but the second meaning is fishing lines flung out over water.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre directors choose performers at auditions, and anglers fling their hooks into the water; both activities share this one word.

clue.text: Back on route to Hull initially — not south!

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in reverse
initially means at the start, so each word gives only its opening letter

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A traveller heads back on the road to Hull, insisting they are not going south.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is a city in the north of England, so the surface direction is itself the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The compass point opposite south is north, so anything not heading south can be heading north.

clue.text: Pay vet mostly to turn up, speak and disappear

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so each word loses its final letter
in a down clue turning up flips the letters so they read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the word without its last letter
the word without its last letter
to orate is to make a formal speech

explanation.surface: A pet owner pays the vet, makes a speech and vanishes.
explanation.walkthrough: Both of the first two words are cut short before they are put together and flipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquids evaporate when they turn to vapour and vanish, and figuratively anything that vanishes can be said to do so.

clue.text: Type of sodium? True/false

indicators.note: something false is not genuine, so the letters are a counterfeit arrangement

blocks.note: Na is the chemical symbol for sodium
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chemistry quiz question: what kind of sodium is it, answer true or false?
explanation.walkthrough: The slash makes True/false look like a quiz format; in fact 'True' is the fodder and 'false' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The nature of something is its kind or character, as in 'problems of this nature', so it can mean sort or kind.

clue.text: For each agreement, a drink

blocks.note: per means for each, as in 'per person'
a nod of the head signals agreement

explanation.surface: Each time a deal is agreed, everyone toasts it with a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Pernod is a French brand of aniseed-flavoured spirit, served diluted with water.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a brand of French anise liqueur, an alcoholic beverage, so the clue defines it by category.

clue.text: Examples of species penultimately displaced by humans

indicators.note: displaced means pushed out and replaced, and penultimately pins the one swapped letter to second from the end

blocks.note: taken as written
men as a word for people in general

explanation.surface: Members of various species are being driven out of their habitats by people.
explanation.walkthrough: The E second from the end of species is swapped out for MEN, giving SPECI-MEN-S.
explanation.definitionFit: Specimens are individual samples taken as typical of their kind, so they serve as examples or instances.

clue.text: Right oven should do this

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for right
an oast is a kiln for drying hops

explanation.surface: A proper oven ought to be capable of this job.
explanation.walkthrough: An oast is a kiln for drying hops, familiar from the cone-roofed oast houses of Kent; the whole clue then describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovens cook meat and vegetables with dry heat, which is precisely what a good one is expected to manage.

clue.text: Had dinner in said school

definitions.note: a past form; the answer is the past participle

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the word is judged by how it is pronounced

blocks.note: Eton is the famous English boarding school near Windsor

explanation.surface: Someone ate their dinner at a particular school mentioned earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton College is an elite English private school; its name is pronounced the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Having had dinner means having consumed food, and the participle of 'eat' expresses that completed meal.

clue.text: Nag's comment beginning to bother the Guardian's local resident

indicators.note: a beginning is the start, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: a nag is a horse, and its remark is the sound it makes
the opening letter
this puzzle appears in the Guardian, so the paper's own is ours

explanation.surface: A nagging remark starts to irritate the person who lives nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: Nag sounds like a complaining person, but it is an old horse. Setters use the paper's name to mean 'our'.
explanation.definitionFit: The person living next door or nearby is a fellow local resident, which is what this word denotes.

clue.text: At the end, Spanish flu victim lost blood and so made to feel bad

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so each of the next words gives its last one

blocks.note: the final letters of these three words
to bleed is to lose blood

explanation.surface: A victim of the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic suffered bleeding and felt dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: Spanish flu looks like a single historical phrase, but each of its words, plus victim, contributes just a last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Being humbled means being brought low and made to feel small or ashamed, a lowering of one's self-esteem.

clue.text: Email, when sloshed at the same time

indicators.note: sloshed means drunk, and drunken letters reel into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, nine letters

explanation.surface: A warning about sending messages while drunk and doing two things at once.
explanation.walkthrough: Sloshed is British slang for drunk, a common anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This adverb means during the intervening time or simultaneously, so it can stand for concurrently happening events.

clue.text: Bug an Ingrid or Heidi, perhaps

blocks.note: a germ is a bug in the sense of an infection
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wants to pester a woman named Ingrid or Heidi.
explanation.walkthrough: Bug looks like a verb meaning to annoy, but it is the noun for a microbe. 'Perhaps' warns that the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingrid and Heidi are typical given names in Germany, so a woman so named might well be from that country.

clue.text: Instruments for court officials

blocks.note: first meaning: simple woodwind pipes often learnt at school
second meaning: part-time judges in English courts

explanation.walkthrough: In England and Wales a recorder is a barrister or solicitor who sits as a part-time judge.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both school woodwind pipes and part-time judges in the English legal system, two unrelated senses.

clue.text: Playing spades is approved

indicators.note: playing about with things moves them around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A card player's lead of spades has been sanctioned by the table.
explanation.walkthrough: Passed is also a bridge call, which helps the card-game surface hide the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A motion or law that is passed has been formally voted through and sanctioned, so it has been approved.

clue.text: Down payment is back in store

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in reverse
in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
a depot is a storehouse or warehouse

explanation.surface: A customer's down payment has been returned to them at the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Store reads as a shop, but it is a warehouse, which becomes the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A deposit is a first instalment paid upfront to secure a purchase, the standard meaning of a down payment.

clue.text: They say take in bird food and be a winner!

indicators.note: what people say is spoken aloud, so the words are judged by their pronunciation

blocks.note: to suck is to take in, and birdseed is bird food

explanation.surface: A tongue-in-cheek motivational slogan: swallow some birdseed and you will triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: The two-word phrase spoken quickly produces the single word.
explanation.definitionFit: To succeed is to achieve one's aim or triumph, which is what a winner does.

clue.text: Butter, jam, or marmalade and many other things on the table

definitions.text: many other things on the table

blocks.note: first meaning: something smeared on bread or toast

blocks.clueFragment: many other things on the table
blocks.note: second meaning: a lavish array of food laid out for a meal

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads like one breakfast table, but it splits after the list into a second meaning: a generous laid-out feast.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything smeared onto toast is this, and so is a lavish buffet laid out for guests to share.

clue.text: Most boring Washington DC airport, plus its terminal?

indicators.note: a terminal is an end point, so only the last letter is kept

blocks.note: Dulles International is the main airport serving Washington DC
its refers back to the airport, whose final letter is taken

explanation.surface: A traveller rates a Washington airport the most tedious, terminal building included.
explanation.walkthrough: Terminal suggests an airport building, but it means the last letter of 'airport'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull means boring, and the superlative of dull is the most boring of all.

clue.text: Trendy fish found underfoot?

definitions.note: describes the thing rather than naming it

blocks.note: something in is fashionable
a sole is a flatfish

explanation.surface: A fashionable fish turns up somewhere surprising, beneath someone's foot.
explanation.walkthrough: The fish is also a word for the underside of a foot, which fits the definition nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: An insole is the inner cushioned layer of a shoe that the foot rests on, so it lies beneath the wearer's foot.

clue.text: Modern resort appears regularly in the Times?

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: modern means new
a spa is a health resort
the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A new seaside resort keeps showing up in the Times.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals a definition by example: The Times is one British daily.
explanation.definitionFit: The Times is a long-established London daily, one example of a printed publication carrying news.

clue.text: Coins from church supporting writer

indicators.note: in a down clue a support sits underneath, so this piece goes below the other

blocks.note: a pen is a writing instrument
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church donates money to support an author.
explanation.walkthrough: Writer suggests a person, but it is the pen itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Pence is the plural of penny, the small British coin, so the word names a set of coins.

clue.text: Right river for country

definitions.note: used as an adjective, as in country life

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for right
the Ural flows from Russia through Kazakhstan to the Caspian

explanation.surface: Choosing the correct river for a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Country looks like a noun meaning nation, but it is the adjective for the countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: Rural describes the countryside as opposed to towns, which is the adjectival sense of country, as in country life.

clue.text: Poetry heard in prime time

indicators.note: in points inside the following word, where the letters sit
what is heard is listened to, so the letters count by their sound

blocks.note: four letters sit inside this phrase, starting after its first letter, and they sound like the answer

explanation.surface: Verse is being broadcast in a peak-hour television slot.
explanation.walkthrough: Rime, frost, sits inside the word prime; said aloud it is identical to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyme is used loosely for verse in general, as in 'nursery rhyme', so it can mean poetry.

clue.text: After love, one is overwhelmed by French rejection — it's a tear-jerker

indicators.note: to be overwhelmed is to be engulfed, so one piece is swallowed inside another
after places what follows behind, so this piece comes second

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
one is the Roman numeral I
non is French for no

explanation.surface: A heartbroken lover is turned down by a French partner and weeps.
explanation.walkthrough: Tear-jerker sounds like a sad film, but it is the vegetable whose chopping makes eyes water.
explanation.definitionFit: Slicing this bulb releases a compound that stings the eyes and makes people cry, hence a humorous tear-jerker.

clue.text: Useful in case of flat or round belly

blocks.note: first meaning: the extra wheel carried for a puncture
second meaning: a roll of fat around the waist

explanation.walkthrough: Flat suggests a home or a flat stomach, the opposite of a round belly; it is a punctured tyre.
explanation.definitionFit: Motorists carry an extra wheel for punctures, and British slang uses the same phrase for a ring of fat around the waist.

clue.text: Some severe storm would impede climbing it

definitions.text: Some severe storm would impede climbing it

indicators.note: some means a portion, so the letters are a part of the phrase that follows

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Bad weather would make an ascent of this mountain difficult.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer while also containing it; 'it' stands for the mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: The world's highest peak is notorious for blizzards that halt expeditions, so a storm would hinder any ascent.

clue.text: Look, new space suit at last

indicators.note: something new is remade, so these letters take a fresh order
at last means at the end, so only the final letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter

explanation.surface: An astronaut shows off a brand-new space suit at long last.
explanation.walkthrough: Look is the noun meaning appearance, not the command to see.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspect is the appearance or outward expression of something, as in 'a gloomy aspect', so a look.
